We traditionally treat noise as the enemy of coherence, and counter it either by isolating the system better or by correcting its errors~\cite{Acharya2023}. A complementary route asks what the environment can actually \emph{see}. Figure~\ref{fig:model} (a) illustrates this distinction. Independent noise channels resolve the coupled spin component at each site, whereas a collective field couples only to their sum. Spatial correlations in the environment therefore determine how well it can distinguish different spin configurations. Decoherence-free subspaces and noiseless subsystems exploit collective coupling to preserve quantum information~\cite{Zanardi1997,Lidar1998,Knill2000}. Correlated dephasing has also been measured in trapped-ion, superconducting and silicon-spin devices~\cite{Monz2011,vonLupke2020,Yoneda2023}. Our earlier work showed that a shared correlated environment can synchronize two coupled spins~\cite{Tyagi2024} and coupled quantum oscillators~\cite{Bittner2025jcp}. These studies explored how environmental correlations can organize collective quantum dynamics. We now carry this question into an interacting many-body system. Can a correlated environment protect entanglement that the system generates intrinsically, starting from an unentangled state? What fixes its surviving amount, and can it be used to perform a quantum task?

Strong symmetries also organize dissipative dynamics into invariant sectors~\cite{BucaProsen2012}. For unital channels with non-Abelian on-site symmetries, maximally mixed invariant-sector states can be entangled and have distillable entanglement~\cite{Moharramipour2024}. These results motivate a concrete question for spatial symmetries: can a driven ring prepare such a mixed resource from a product state, and can operations on physical spins expose its usefulness? The extraction question is related to localizable entanglement, which studies entanglement localized between spins by measurements on the others~\cite{Popp2005}. Here we allow coherent gates within each half of the ring and specify one heralded filter, without optimizing over all such operations.

The spatial symmetries of the spin chain, which here forms a ring, act together with collective dephasing to protect part of this entanglement in the stationary state. We then extract an entangled pair of physical spins by local operations confined to the separate halves and use the pair for teleportation above the classical fidelity benchmark. Figure~\ref{fig:model}(b) illustrates how correlated noise protects the generated entanglement and how that entanglement can subsequently be used. Once this entangled steady state is reached, neither the coherent driving nor the collective dephasing changes it.
new: \emph{In this Letter} we connect spatial-symmetry-restricted noisy dynamics to a physical teleportation resource in a driven Ising ring~\cite{Bertini2018}. The protecting transformations permute ring sites, rather than acting as the on-site symmetry considered in Ref.~\cite{Moharramipour2024}. Starting from a uniform product state, interactions generate entanglement. Collective dephasing preserves the ring-symmetric sector containing that input, and the driven dynamics approaches a maximally mixed density within this sector. For twelve spins, a fixed decoder confined to the two separate halves extracts an entangled pair of physical spins and uses it for teleportation above the classical fidelity benchmark. Figure~\ref{fig:model}(b) shows the extraction and subsequent task. The contribution is this explicit preparation-to-task connection, with separately quantified accepted-pair fidelity and extraction probability; it does not require every state in the sector to be unchanged by noise.

old: We show that correlated dephasing protects entanglement generated through interactions between the system's degrees of freedom. Symmetries associated with the geometry of the spin-chain determine the final state, and collective noise channels preserve states within the protected sector. Furthermore, this protected entanglement serves as a resource that local decoding can access to perform quantum tasks. The resulting distinction between persistent many-body entanglement and its extraction yield provides a direct route from a symmetry-protected attractor to a testable quantum-information task. This has profound implications for understanding how quantum effects get amplified at scale, for advancing scalable quantum technology, and even for analyzing coherent ransport mechanisms in chemical and biological systems. Natural settings to test this include light-matter experiments, neutral-atom architectures, and light-harvesting complexes—essentially any quantum simulator that allows tunable collective modes to couple to the system.
new: We show that collective dephasing protects entanglement generated by interactions from an initially unentangled product state. In the twelve-spin ring, collective noise preserves the ring-symmetric sector, within which the driven dynamics approaches an entangled stationary density. This density is unchanged by each coherent layer and by collective dephasing; preservation of the sector does not imply invariance of every supported state. A fixed decoder acting separately within the two halves extracts a physical pair that implements teleportation with uniform-input average fidelity $19/21$ and heralding probability $1/192$. The fidelity characterizes the quality of the accepted pairs, while the probability determines their extraction yield; their physical production rate depends on the implementation. The example connects a symmetry-protected many-body stationary state to a concrete quantum-information task and distinguishes persistent entanglement from the yield of an accessible resource.
